question.text:
A 53-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, recurrent diarrhea, and an 8-kg (17.6-lb) weight loss over the past 6 months. He has a 4-month history of recurrent blistering rashes on different parts of his body that grow and develop into pruritic, crusty lesions before resolving spontaneously. Physical examination shows scaly lesions in different phases of healing with central, bronze-colored induration around the mouth, perineum, and lower extremities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 10.1 mg/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 85 μm3
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin 30.0 pg/cell
Serum
Glucose 236 mg/dL
Abdominal ultrasonography shows a 3-cm, solid mass located in the upper abdomen. This patient's mass is most likely derived from which of the following types of cells?"

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's presentation of fatigue, diarrhea, weight loss, recurrent blistering rashes, and bronze-colored induration around the mouth, perineum, and lower extremities strongly suggests MEN 1 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1). The abdominal ultrasound finding of a 3-cm solid mass in the upper abdomen further supports this diagnosis. MEN 1 is characterized by tumors of the parathyroid glands, pituitary gland, and pancreas. The pancreatic tumors in MEN 1 are most commonly gastrinomas (A), which produce excessive gastrin leading to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES). ZES is characterized by severe peptic ulcers, diarrhea, and weight loss. The bronze-colored induration around the mouth, perineum, and lower extremities is a classic sign of ZES.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Bronze-colored induration around the mouth, perineum, and lower extremities is a classic sign of ZES, which is associated with gastrinomas.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Pancreatic α-cells (B) produce glucagon, which can cause diabetes, but the presentation is not typical. Pancreatic β-cells (C) produce insulin, which can cause diabetes, but the presentation is not typical. Pancreatic δ-cells (D) produce somatostatin, which can cause diabetes and steatorrhea, but the presentation is not typical. Gastric G-cells (E) produce gastrin, which can cause ZES, but the presentation is not typical.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's clinical presentation of recurrent blistering rashes with pruritus and crusty lesions, along with the abdominal mass, suggests a possible neoplasm. The elevated serum glucose level (236 mg/dL) and the presence of a solid mass in the upper abdomen raise suspicion for a pancreatic origin. Pancreatic α-cells secrete glucagon, which would lead to hyperglycemia, and their neoplasms can present with abdominal masses. The other options (β-cells, δ-cells, and G-cells) secrete insulin, somatostatin, and gastrin respectively, which are less likely to cause the observed symptoms and findings.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered pancreatic β-cell tumor (insulinoma) due to hyperinsulinemia, but ruled out due to normal glucose level. G-cell tumor was considered but less likely due to typical symptoms of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Pancreatic δ-cell tumor was considered but somatostatinoma is rare and typically presents differently. Enterochromaffin cells are more associated with carcinoid syndrome.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with fatigue, weight loss, recurrent diarrhea, and a 3-cm abdominal mass, along with characteristic skin lesions (blistering, pruritic, crusty) and hyperglycemia (glucose 236 mg/dL). These findings are classic for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which is caused by gastrin-secreting tumors (gastrinomas) typically arising from the pancreas. Gastrinomas are derived from pancreatic β-cells, which can aberrantly produce gastrin. The skin lesions are consistent with acrodermatitis enteropathica or other paraneoplastic syndromes, but the key diagnostic clue is the hyperglycemia and diarrhea due to excessive gastric acid secretion from gastrin excess. The abdominal mass is most likely a gastrinoma, which originates from pancreatic β-cells.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Hyperglycemia (glucose 236 mg/dL) and recurrent diarrhea suggest excessive gastric acid secretion, consistent with gastrinoma, which arises from pancreatic β-cells.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other pancreatic endocrine tumors (e.g., insulinoma, glucagonoma) were considered, but the hyperglycemia and diarrhea point to gastrin excess, not insulin deficiency or glucagon excess. Gastrointestinal enterochromaffin cells (A) are associated with carcinoid tumors, which typically cause diarrhea but not hyperglycemia. Pancreatic α-cells (B) and δ-cells (D) produce glucagon and somatostatin, respectively, and are not associated with gastrin excess or the described skin lesions. Gastric G-cells (E) are not typically associated with abdominal masses or systemic hyperglycemia.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Pancreatic β-cell (insulinoma), pancreatic α-cell (glucagonoma), and gastric G-cell (gastrinoma) tumors were considered but do not typically cause the described skin lesions. C and D are less likely because vasoactive peptide excess can cause cutaneous flushing and pruritus, but the mass and weight loss are more characteristic of a neuroendocrine tumor like a carcinoid, which often originate from enterochromaffin cells.
